p: Good evening, my dear friend, and welcome to the ridge. Base camp was number; the foothills were algebra. Now the path runs along a high ridge with views in every direction, and its name is functions and graphs. A graph is a picture, and we are working by ear, so tonight I shall teach you to see graphs in your mind's eye, and to describe them in words, which is a fine skill even for those with perfect sight.
## The grid

Imagine a sheet of squared paper. Draw a line straight across the middle, from left to right: this is the x axis. Draw another straight up the middle: the y axis. Where they cross is the origin, the point nought, nought.

Every point on the sheet can be described by two numbers. How far across from the origin, to the right for positive and left for negative: that is x. How far up, or down for negative: that is y. We write them in round brackets with a comma: x first, then y.
Three across, two up. The order matters: x first, as in the saying, along the corridor and then up the stairs.
?? While I pour. Describe the position of the point minus four, comma, one.
=> Four to the left of the origin, and one up.
## Descartes and the fly

These are called Cartesian coordinates, after René Descartes, who published the idea in 1637 in La Géométrie, an appendix to his Discourse on Method. Pierre de Fermat had the same idea at about the same time, independently. Their great insight was that every equation in x and y describes a shape, and every shape can be described by an equation. Algebra and geometry became one subject.

There is a charming story that Descartes, lying in bed watching a fly crawl on the ceiling, realised he could describe its position by its distances from two walls. He did like to stay in bed late in the mornings, but the fly is a legend, and I would not swear to it in court.
## A graph is a picture of a rule
Take the rule: y equals two x.

When x is nought, y is nought. When x is one, y is two. When x is two, y is four. When x is minus one, y is minus two. Mark all those points, and they lie on a straight line through the origin, rising steeply as it goes to the right: two steps up for every step across. The graph is the picture of every pair x, y that obeys the rule.
## Describing a graph in words

Here is how I describe a graph aloud, and I recommend it to you. First, its general shape: straight or curved. Second, which way it goes as you move left to right: rising, falling or level. Third, where it crosses the axes. Fourth, anything special: a highest or lowest point, a place where it levels off, or a place where it shoots off towards infinity.

The graph of y equals x squared, for example: a U-shaped curve, called a parabola, symmetrical about the y axis, with its lowest point at the origin. It falls as you approach from the left, touches nought, and rises again, ever more steeply.
?? Describe the graph of y equals three. What do you think it looks like?
=> y is three whatever x is: a level straight line, three units above the x axis.
## Hearing a graph

Some of my colleagues in the library of the future have made graphs audible: as you move from left to right, a tone rises in pitch when the graph goes up and falls when it goes down. Our own app uses tones in a similar spirit for the depth of brackets. If you like, imagine y equals x squared as a whistle that starts high, swoops down to a low note in the middle, and swoops back up.
## Reading a real graph

Graphs carry real information. A graph of temperature through a day rises from a low before dawn to a peak in mid-afternoon, then falls through the evening. A graph of the cost of a cab ride starts above nought, the fixed charge, and rises steadily, by the same amount for every mile. A graph of a falling apple's height curves downwards, slowly at first, then faster.

Florence Nightingale, whom you will meet in the lectures on statistics, used diagrams to persuade the government that soldiers in the Crimean War were dying more of disease than of wounds. A good picture can change policy.
## Where graphs cross

If you draw two graphs on the same grid, the points where they cross are the points that satisfy both rules at once. Remember simultaneous equations? The solution x equals seven and y equals three of x plus y equals ten and x minus y equals four is precisely where those two straight lines cross.
## Summary

The grid has an x axis across and a y axis up, crossing at the origin. A point is written x comma y in round brackets, across then up. A graph is the picture of every pair obeying a rule. Describe a graph by its shape, direction, crossings and special points. Descartes and Fermat married algebra and geometry. Next time, straight lines: gradient and intercept. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight the central idea of the ridge, and indeed of the whole of higher mathematics: the function. A function is a machine. You put a number in; it does something to it; a number comes out. That is all. But from that simple notion grows almost everything at the summit.
## The machine

Picture a brass machine on my desk, rather like one of Mr Babbage's, with a hopper on top and a chute below. Into the hopper I drop a number. Inside, the machine doubles it and adds one. Out of the chute rolls the answer. Drop in three, out comes seven. Drop in ten, out comes twenty-one. Drop in nought, out comes one.
We give the machine a name, usually f, for function, and write its rule like this:

In plain words: f of x equals two x plus one. The letter x stands for whatever goes in. f of x, said f of x, means what comes out when x goes in. It does not mean f times x; the brackets here are the hopper, not a multiplication.
f of three equals seven.
?? While I pour. If g of x equals x squared minus two, what is g of five?
=> Five squared is twenty-five, minus two is twenty-three.
## Exactly one output

The one strict rule: for each input, a function gives exactly one output. A machine that sometimes gave seven and sometimes eight for the same input would be no use at all; Mrs Blewitt would return it to the shop. Different inputs may give the same output; that is allowed. The squaring machine turns both three and minus three into nine. But one input must never give two outputs.
## A brief history

The word function was used by Leibniz in the 1690s, for quantities connected to a curve. Leonhard Euler, in 1734, introduced the notation f of x, and in 1748 defined a function as an analytic expression made up of a variable and constants. In 1837 the German mathematician Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet gave the modern, very general idea: any rule at all that assigns exactly one output to each input, whether or not it has a neat formula. So the function is a young idea, younger than the steam engine, and it grew up in my own century.
## Domain and range
The domain is the set of inputs the machine accepts. The range is the set of outputs that can come out.

The square-root machine, if we stick to ordinary numbers, will not accept negative inputs. Its domain is nought and the positive numbers. The machine f of x equals one over x will not accept nought, because you cannot divide by nought: put in nought and the machine jams, steam everywhere.
?? What is the range of the squaring machine, f of x equals x squared?
=> Nought and the positive numbers. A square is never negative.
## Many ways to describe a function

A function can be given by a formula, by a table, by a graph, or in words. The cab fare: one pound plus fifty pence per mile. That is a function of the miles. The temperature at noon each day is a function of the date, though no neat formula describes it. Your age in years is a function of today's date. A function needs a rule, not necessarily a formula.
## The graph
The graph of a function is the picture of all the pairs x and f of x, with f of x playing the part of y. So the graph of f of x equals two x plus one is the straight line y equals two x plus one.

There is a neat test for whether a graph shows a function, the vertical line test. Imagine a vertical line sliding across the picture from left to right. If it ever crosses the graph twice at once, one input has two outputs, and it is not a function. A circle fails the test; a parabola passes.
## Functions of functions

Machines can be joined in a chain: the output of one becomes the input of the next. And some machines can be run in reverse. Those are the subjects of my next lecture, composition and inverse functions.
## Functions everywhere

Once you have the idea, you see functions everywhere. The pitch of a note is a function of the length of a string, as the Pythagoreans discovered. The cost of a parcel is a function of its weight. The height of a cannonball is a function of time. At the summit, calculus will ask how fast a function's output changes as its input changes, and how much it adds up to. Everything up there is about functions.
## Summary

A function is a rule, a machine, that turns each input into exactly one output. We write f of x for the output when x goes in. The domain is the set of allowed inputs, the range the set of possible outputs. A function may be a formula, a table, a graph or words, and its graph is the picture of all pairs x and f of x. Euler gave us f of x; Dirichlet gave the modern idea. Next time, chaining machines and running them backwards. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight the humblest graph of all, and the most useful: the straight line. Every straight line has a simple equation, and once you know how to read it, you can picture any line from its equation, and write the equation for any line you can picture.
## Gradient: the steepness

The gradient of a line measures how steep it is: how far up it goes for each single step across. A gentle line might rise a half for each step; a steep line might rise five. The road signs on steep hills in your century, I am told, show a gradient as a percentage; in mine, as one in ten, which means one foot up for every ten along.
⟦m=\frac{\text{rise}}{\text{run}}⟧
In plain words: the gradient, which mathematicians traditionally call m, is the rise over the run. Pick two points on the line, find how far up you go between them, and divide by how far across.
?? While I pour. A line goes from the point one comma two to the point three comma eight. What is its gradient?
=> The rise is eight minus two, six. The run is three minus one, two. Six over two is three.
## Up, down and level

A positive gradient means the line rises as you go from left to right, like walking uphill. A negative gradient means it falls, downhill. A gradient of nought is perfectly level, like the surface of a pond. And a vertical line, a cliff, has no gradient at all: the run is nought, and we cannot divide by nought.
## Intercept: where it crosses
The intercept is the point where the line crosses the y axis, that is, where x is nought. It tells you how high the line is at the start.
## The equation
Put the two together.
$$ y=mx+c
In plain words: y equals m x plus c. m is the gradient, and c is the intercept. Start at height c, and for every one step to the right, rise by m.
This line crosses the y axis at one, and rises two for every step across. When x is three, y is seven.
This line crosses the y axis at four, and falls one for every step across. It crosses the x axis at four, where y is nought.
?? Describe the line y equals half x minus three.
=> It crosses the y axis at minus three, and rises gently, a half for each step across.
## Lines in daily life
Our hansom cab fare from an earlier lecture, one pound plus fifty pence a mile, is a straight line: intercept one, the fixed charge, and gradient a half, the cost per mile.

Converting temperatures is a straight line too: Fahrenheit equals nine fifths Celsius plus thirty-two. Gradient nine fifths, intercept thirty-two. Whenever one quantity grows at a steady rate as another grows, the graph is a straight line, and the relationship is called linear.
## Parallel lines

Two lines with the same gradient are parallel. They rise at the same rate, so they never meet, like the rails of the Great Western Railway, which Mr Brunel laid at his famous broad gauge of seven feet and a quarter inch. y equals two x plus one, and y equals two x minus five, are parallel. Different intercepts, same steepness.
Remember from simultaneous equations: parallel lines never cross, so their equations have no common solution.
## Finding the equation of a line

Given two points, find the gradient as rise over run. Then put one point into y equals m x plus c to find c. For the points one comma two and three comma eight, the gradient is three. So y equals three x plus c. Put in x equals one and y equals two: two equals three plus c, so c is minus one. The line is y equals three x minus one. Check with the other point: three times three minus one is eight. Splendid.
?? A line has gradient two and passes through the point two comma seven. What is c?
=> Seven equals two times two plus c, so c is three. The line is y equals two x plus three.
## Summary

Gradient is rise over run: positive uphill, negative downhill, nought level. The intercept c is where the line meets the y axis. Every non-vertical line is y equals m x plus c. Parallel lines share a gradient. Any steady rate of change gives a straight line. Next time, functions: the number machines that every graph is a picture of. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Last time we met the function, a machine that turns inputs into outputs. Tonight, two pieces of machinery for the workshop: joining machines end to end, and running a machine backwards. Both will be essential at the summit; the chain rule of calculus is all about the first.
## Composite functions
Take two machines. f adds three. g doubles.
Now feed five into g: out comes ten. Feed that ten straight into f: out comes thirteen. We write the combined machine as f of g of x.
Read it from the inside out: the innermost brackets go first, just as in the primer on brackets. g acts first, then f. Like getting dressed: put on a shirt, then a waistcoat.
?? While I pour. With the same machines, what is f of g of four?
=> g doubles four to eight, then f adds three: eleven.
## Order matters
Now try g of f of x: f first, then g. Five goes into f: eight. Eight goes into g: sixteen. Not thirteen.

So the order of machines matters. Adding three and then doubling is not the same as doubling and then adding three. In the same way, putting on your socks and then your boots is not the same as your boots and then your socks, as any small child can demonstrate.
?? With f adding three and g doubling, what is g of f of nought?
=> f turns nought into three, and g doubles it: six.
## Inverse functions

Now run a machine backwards. If f turns three into seven, the inverse machine turns seven back into three. We write it f inverse, with a little minus one raised, like a power, though it is not a power.
In plain words: f inverse of seven is three.

To find an inverse by thinking: list what the machine does, in order, then undo each step, in reverse order. The machine f of x equals two x plus one first doubles, then adds one. To undo, first take away one, then halve.

Check: f turns three into seven; f inverse turns seven into seven minus one, six, halved, three. Back home. This is exactly what we did when solving equations and rearranging formulas: undo in reverse order, coat before waistcoat.
?? What is the inverse of the machine that multiplies by three and then subtracts four?
=> First add four, then divide by three: x plus four, all over three.
## An algebra method

There is also a mechanical method. Write y equals f of x, rearrange to make x the subject, then rename. For y equals two x plus one: y minus one equals two x, so x equals y minus one over two. Swap the names, and f inverse of x is x minus one over two.
## Not every machine can be reversed

The squaring machine turns both three and minus three into nine. Given nine, which should the reverse machine return? It cannot know. A function has an inverse only if each output comes from just one input. For squaring, we usually agree to accept only positive inputs, and then the inverse is the square root.
## The mirror

Here is a pretty picture. Draw the graph of a function and the graph of its inverse on the same grid. They are mirror images of each other in the diagonal line y equals x, the line through the origin at forty-five degrees. Because the inverse swaps inputs and outputs, it swaps x and y, and swapping x and y is reflecting in that diagonal.
## Inverses you already know

Subtracting undoes adding. Dividing undoes multiplying. Square roots undo squares, for positive numbers. In trigonometry, the inverse tangent undoes the tangent, turning a ratio back into an angle. And soon you will meet logarithms, which undo powers. John Napier's invention of logarithms, as you will hear, was in effect the discovery of an inverse function a century before anyone had the word.
## Summary

A composite function chains machines: f of g of x means g first, then f, from the inside out. Order matters. An inverse function undoes a function, found by undoing each step in reverse order, or by rearranging. Only one-to-one functions have inverses, and the graph of the inverse is the mirror image in y equals x. Next, quadratics, starting with factorising. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Throw a ball across a lawn and watch its path: it rises, slows, turns over at the top and falls, in a smooth and perfectly symmetrical arch. Galileo showed, in his book of 1638, that, ignoring the air, that arch is a parabola, the graph of a quadratic. Tonight we learn to see it in the mind's eye.
## The simplest parabola

Picture it, as we did in the lecture on graphs. When x is nought, y is nought. When x is one or minus one, y is one. When x is two or minus two, y is four. Three or minus three, nine. A U shape, its lowest point at the origin, perfectly symmetrical about the y axis, the two arms rising ever more steeply.

The lowest point is called the vertex, or the turning point. The vertical line through it, here the y axis, is the line of symmetry. Fold the paper along it and the two arms lie exactly on top of each other.
## Upside down

Put a minus sign in front, and every y becomes negative: the U turns upside down, like an arch or a thrown ball. Its vertex is now the highest point. The rule: if the number in front of x squared is positive, the parabola smiles; if it is negative, it frowns.
?? While I pour. Does y equals minus three x squared plus x open upwards or downwards?
=> Downwards. The coefficient of x squared is minus three, negative.
## Narrow and wide
Multiply by three and every height triples: the U becomes narrower and steeper. Multiply by a half, and it becomes wider and gentler, a shallow dish.
## Shifting about
Adding two lifts the whole curve up two. The vertex moves to nought, two.

This one is subtler. The bracket is nought, and so y is smallest, when x is three. So the vertex has moved three to the right. Notice: minus three in the bracket moves it right, not left. People find this backwards at first. Think of it as: x must be three before the bracket reaches nought.
Combine them, and the vertex is at three, two. This is why completing the square is so useful: it puts any quadratic into this form and reveals its vertex at once.
?? Where is the vertex of y equals, bracket x plus one, squared, minus four?
=> The bracket is nought when x is minus one, and then y is minus four. The vertex is at minus one, minus four.
## Where it crosses the axes

The parabola crosses the y axis where x is nought: just put nought in. It crosses the x axis where y is nought: and that means solving the quadratic equation. So the roots of a quadratic are where its parabola meets the x axis.

Take y equals x squared minus five x plus six. It crosses the y axis at six. It crosses the x axis at two and three, the roots we found by factorising. And the vertex lies exactly halfway between the roots, at two and a half, by symmetry.
## The discriminant, pictured

Now the discriminant makes visual sense. A smiling parabola whose vertex dips below the x axis crosses it twice: two roots. One whose vertex just touches the axis: one root. One whose vertex sits above the axis never reaches it: no ordinary roots. The formula and the picture tell the same story.
?? The vertex of a smiling parabola is at two, five. How many times does it cross the x axis?
=> None. Its lowest point is five above the axis.
## Parabolas in the world

A fountain's jet. The cables of a suspension bridge carrying a level roadway are very nearly parabolas. A parabolic mirror sends every ray of light from its focus out in a straight parallel beam, which is why lighthouse reflectors and, I am informed, motor-car headlamps are shaped so. The Greeks studied the parabola as a slice through a cone; Apollonius of Perga, around two hundred years before Christ, gave it its name.
## Summary

A quadratic's graph is a parabola: smiling if the x squared coefficient is positive, frowning if negative, narrower for larger coefficients. In the form, x minus h, squared, plus k, the vertex is at h, k. The roots are where it meets the x axis, and the vertex is halfway between them. Next, sequences: patterns that go on and on. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight we meet the function that runs compound interest, epidemics, the cooling of tea and, I am told, the growth of the little glass slates themselves. It is the exponential function, and its signature is this: it grows not by adding the same amount each time, but by multiplying.
## Adding versus multiplying

Two ways to grow. Linear growth adds a fixed amount each step: ten, twenty, thirty, forty. Its graph is a straight line. Exponential growth multiplies by a fixed factor each step: ten, twenty, forty, eighty, a hundred and sixty. At first the two keep company. Then the multiplying one leaves the other standing.
In plain words: y equals a times b to the power of x. Here a is the starting amount, b the factor applied in each step, and x the number of steps. If b is two, it doubles each step.
?? While I pour. A colony of a hundred cells doubles every hour. How many after five hours?
=> A hundred times two to the power of five: a hundred times thirty-two, three thousand two hundred.
## The graph

Picture y equals two to the power of x. To the left, for negative x, it lies very close to the x axis, just above it, never touching: a half, a quarter, an eighth. It crosses the y axis at one, since anything to the power of nought is one. Then it climbs, slowly, then steeply, then almost straight upwards. Its steepness at any point is proportional to its height. That last fact will matter enormously at the summit.
## Compound interest

Mr Micawber, you may remember from an earlier lecture, had views on income and expenditure. Here is a matter he should have considered. Put a hundred pounds in a bank at five per cent a year, compound. Each year it is multiplied by one point nought five. After ten years: a hundred times one point nought five to the power of ten, about a hundred and sixty-three pounds. After fourteen years or so, it has doubled. The rule of seventy-two says: divide seventy-two by the percentage rate to get roughly the doubling time. Seventy-two divided by five is fourteen and a bit.
## Malthus

In 1798 the Reverend Thomas Malthus argued, in his Essay on the Principle of Population, that population, if unchecked, grows geometrically, that is, exponentially, while food supply grows only arithmetically, by addition. Misery, he concluded, must follow. Charles Darwin read Malthus in 1838 and later wrote that it gave him the idea of natural selection. Malthus's gloomy prediction did not come true in the form he expected, largely because farming improved enormously, but his mathematics was a sharp tool.
## Decay

If the factor is less than one, the quantity shrinks. Multiply by a half each step, and you have halving: a hundred, fifty, twenty-five, twelve and a half. The time taken to halve is called the half-life. The library of the future tells me that the radioactive elements, discovered at the very end of my century, decay in exactly this way, each with its own half-life, from fractions of a second to thousands of millions of years. Carbon-fourteen has a half-life of about five thousand seven hundred years, which is how archaeologists date old bones.

A cup of tea cools in a similar fashion: the difference between its temperature and the room's shrinks exponentially. This is Newton's law of cooling. I confess I prove it nightly, by forgetting my tea while writing these lectures.
?? A substance has a half-life of ten years. What fraction remains after thirty years?
=> Three half-lives: a half, a quarter, an eighth. One eighth remains.
## The number e

Now a famous puzzle, studied by Jacob Bernoulli in 1683. Suppose a generous bank offers a hundred per cent interest a year. A pound becomes two pounds. Suppose instead it pays fifty per cent every half year: one point five squared, two pounds and a quarter. Every quarter: one point two five to the power of four, about two point four four. Every month, every day, every second? The amount grows, but not without limit. It settles towards a number about two point seven one eight.
$$ e=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^{n}\approx 2.71828

In plain words: e is the limit, as n grows without end, of one plus one over n, all to the power of n. About two point seven one eight two eight. Leonhard Euler gave it the letter e, around 1731. It is the natural base for growth that is happening continually, all the time, rather than in jumps, and it will be the hero of several lectures at the summit.
## Summary

Exponential functions multiply by a fixed factor each step: y equals a times b to the x. They grow slowly, then explosively, or decay towards nought, with a fixed doubling time or half-life. Compound interest, populations, radioactivity and cooling tea all follow them. Compounding continually leads to the number e, about two point seven one eight. Next, the function that runs exponentials backwards: the logarithm. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. Tonight the logarithm, which many people meet at school as a mysterious button and then forget. In my day it was not a button but a book, a thick volume of tables that every engineer, navigator and actuary kept on the desk, and it saved more drudgery than any invention before Mr Babbage's. Let me show you what it is, and why it was such a blessing.
## The question a logarithm answers
Ten to the power of three is a thousand. Turn that around: to what power must ten be raised to give a thousand? Three. That answer is called the logarithm of a thousand, to base ten.
In plain words: log base ten of a thousand is three. The logarithm undoes the power. It is the inverse function of the exponential, just as subtraction undoes addition.
?? While I pour. What is log base ten of a hundred? And of one?
=> A hundred is ten squared, so two. One is ten to the power of nought, so nought.
Other bases work the same way. Two to the power of five is thirty-two, so log base two of thirty-two is five.
## The great trick: multiplying by adding

Here is why logarithms mattered. Remember the first law of indices: when you multiply powers of the same base, you add the indices. A hundred times a thousand is ten squared times ten cubed, which is ten to the five. So the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms.
$$ \log(ab)=\log a+\log b
In plain words: the log of a times b is the log of a plus the log of b.

So to multiply two awkward numbers, such as three thousand seven hundred and forty-one by eight hundred and twenty-six, you look up their logarithms in the tables, add them, which is easy, and look up which number has that sum as its logarithm. A long multiplication becomes an addition and three look-ups. Division becomes subtraction. Square roots become halving. For astronomers with thousands of multiplications of seven-figure numbers, this was liberation.
## John Napier

John Napier, Laird of Merchiston, near Edinburgh, was a Scottish landowner, a fierce Protestant writer on the Book of Revelation, and an inventor; he proposed various military devices, and local legend credited him with sorcery. In 1614, after some twenty years of calculation, he published his Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio, a description of the marvellous canon of logarithms. He coined the word logarithm, from Greek words meaning ratio and number. His logarithms were not quite ours; they were built on a different and rather complicated scheme.
## Henry Briggs

Henry Briggs, professor of geometry at Gresham College in London, read the book and was overwhelmed. He travelled to Edinburgh in 1615 to meet Napier, and the two agreed that logarithms based on ten would be far more convenient. There is an account, written down many years later, by the astrologer William Lilly, that when they met they gazed at each other in silent admiration for almost a quarter of an hour before either spoke. I tell it to you as a good story, not as sworn history. Napier died in 1617, and Briggs produced the base-ten tables, published in 1617 and, much enlarged, in 1624.

The French mathematician Laplace is reported to have said that logarithms, by shortening the labours, doubled the life of the astronomer. Whether he said precisely that, I cannot vouch, but no astronomer would have disagreed.
## The slide rule

In the 1620s, the English clergyman William Oughtred arranged logarithmic scales on rulers that slide against each other, so that adding lengths multiplies numbers. The slide rule was the engineer's companion for over three hundred years; Mr Brunel would have used one. The library of the future tells me that men flew to the moon with slide rules in their pockets, though the calculations that mattered most were done by electronic machines.
## Logarithms everywhere

Some scales of measurement are logarithmic, because nature spans huge ranges. In music, each octave doubles the frequency, so our ears hear frequencies on a logarithmic scale. The loudness of sound in decibels, the acidity of a liquid on the pH scale, and the strength of earthquakes are all logarithmic: each step up multiplies, rather than adds.
?? If one sound is ten decibels louder than another, its intensity is ten times greater. What about twenty decibels louder?
=> Two steps of ten: ten times ten, a hundred times the intensity.
## Natural logarithms

The logarithm to base e, the number from last time, is called the natural logarithm, written l n. It may seem an odd choice of base, but at the summit you will see why it is natural: it is the one whose rate of change is simplest. Napier's own logarithms, curiously, were closely related to it.
## Summary

A logarithm is the power to which a base must be raised to give a number: it undoes exponentials. The log of a product is the sum of the logs, which turned multiplication into addition. Napier published logarithms in 1614, Briggs made base-ten tables, and Oughtred put them on a slide rule. Next, the wave: sines and cosines as functions. Good night, my dear friend.

Good evening, my dear friend. In the lecture on trigonometry, sine and cosine were ratios in a right-angled triangle, and angles stopped at ninety degrees. Tonight we set them free. We let the angle turn as far as it likes, round and round, and discover that sine and cosine describe every wave in nature: sound, light, tides, the swing of a pendulum and the hum of a tuning fork.
## The wheel

Picture a wheel of radius one, with its centre at the origin of our grid. A painted spot starts on the rim at the far right, level with the centre. Now the wheel turns anticlockwise. As it turns through an angle, the spot rises. Its height above the centre is the sine of the angle. Its distance to the right of the centre is the cosine.
For small angles this agrees with SOH CAH TOA: the hypotenuse is the radius, one, so the opposite side is simply the sine. But now we can keep turning.

At ninety degrees the spot is at the top: height one, sideways nought. So the sine of ninety degrees is one, and the cosine nought. At a hundred and eighty, it is at the far left, level with the centre: sine nought, cosine minus one. At two hundred and seventy, the bottom: sine minus one. At three hundred and sixty, back where it started, and round it goes again.
?? While I pour. What is the cosine of a hundred and eighty degrees?

Degrees are a Babylonian convention. Mathematicians prefer a natural unit, the radian. Walk around the rim of the wheel a distance equal to its radius. The angle you have turned is one radian, a little over fifty-seven degrees. All the way round the rim is two pi radii, so a full turn is two pi radians.

The height of the wave is its amplitude. Three times sine x reaches up to three and down to minus three: a louder sound, a higher tide. A tuning fork, invented in 1711 by John Shore, trumpeter to Queen Anne, sings almost a pure sine wave.

Joseph Fourier, studying the flow of heat, claimed in 1807 that a very wide range of repeating shapes, however jagged, can be built by adding up sine and cosine waves of different frequencies and amplitudes. His book on heat appeared in 1822. Mathematicians argued about exactly when it is true for most of my century, but the idea was right in spirit and enormously powerful. A violin and a flute playing the same note sound different because they add different mixtures of higher sine waves to the main one. $$ y=f(x)+a

Adding a number outside the function lifts every point by that amount. x squared plus three is the same U, lifted three units, with its lowest point at nought, three. Subtracting lowers it. This is the simplest move, and it behaves exactly as you would expect.

$$ y=f(x-a)

Changing the x inside the function moves the graph sideways, and here is the trap: it moves the opposite way to what the sign suggests. x minus three, squared, has its lowest point at x equals three, to the right. Multiplying outside stretches the graph vertically. Two x squared is twice as tall at every point: a narrower, steeper U. A half x squared is squashed down: a wider, shallower dish. Three sine x is a wave three times as tall.
Multiplying x inside squeezes horizontally, and again it works backwards. Sine of two x fits two waves where there used to be one: the wave is squeezed to half its width, not stretched to double.

A minus sign outside, minus f of x, flips the graph upside down: a reflection in the x axis, as though in the still surface of a pond. Minus x squared is the frowning arch.

A minus sign on x, f of minus x, reflects the graph in the y axis, swapping left and right, as in a looking glass. Two to the power of minus x is the decay curve: the mirror image of exponential growth.

Moves can be combined, and the completed-square form of a quadratic shows them all at once.

Some graphs are their own reflections. x squared is unchanged by reflecting in the y axis, since minus x, squared, is x squared: such functions are called even. x cubed is unchanged by a half turn about the origin: called odd. At the summit, calculus will often take a known shape and ask how it changes. Knowing that an unfamiliar formula is merely a familiar graph moved, stretched or flipped saves a great deal of fretting. In mathematics, a function from a set ⟦X⟧ to a set ⟦Y⟧ assigns to each element of ⟦X⟧ exactly one element of ⟦Y⟧. The set ⟦X⟧ is called the domain of the function and the set ⟦Y⟧ is called the codomain of the function.

Functions were originally the idealization of how a varying quantity depends on another quantity. For example, the position of a planet is a function of time. Historically, the concept was elaborated with the infinitesimal calculus at the end of the 17th century, and, until the 19th century, the functions that were considered were differentiable (that is, they had a high degree of regularity). The concept of a function was formalized at the end of the 19th century in terms of set theory, and this greatly increased the possible applications of the concept.

A function is often denoted by a letter such as ⟦f⟧, ⟦g⟧ or ⟦h⟧. The value of a function ⟦f⟧ at an element ⟦x⟧ of its domain (that is, the element of the codomain that is associated with ⟦x⟧) is denoted by ⟦f(x)⟧; for example, the value of ⟦f⟧ at ⟦x = 4⟧ is denoted by ⟦f(4)⟧. Commonly, a specific function is defined by means of an expression depending on ⟦x⟧, such as ⟦f ( x ) = x^{2} + 1 ;⟧ in this case, some computation, called function evaluation, may be needed for deducing the value of the function at a particular value; for example, if ⟦f ( x ) = x^{2} + 1 ,⟧ then ⟦f ( 4 ) = 4^{2} + 1 = 17.⟧

Given its domain and its codomain, a function is uniquely represented by the set of all pairs ⟦(x, f (x))⟧, called the graph of the function, a popular means of illustrating the function. When the domain and the codomain are sets of real numbers, each such pair may be thought of as the Cartesian coordinates of a point in the plane.
Functions are widely used in science, engineering, and in most fields of mathematics. It has been said that functions are "the central objects of investigation" in most fields of mathematics.

The concept of a function has evolved significantly over centuries, from its informal origins in ancient mathematics to its formalization in the 19th century. See History of the function concept for details.
## Definition

A function ⟦f⟧ from a set ⟦X⟧ to a set ⟦Y⟧ is an assignment of one element of ⟦Y⟧ to each element of ⟦X⟧. The set ⟦X⟧ is called the domain of the function and the set ⟦Y⟧ is called the codomain of the function.

If the element ⟦y⟧ in ⟦Y⟧ is assigned to ⟦x⟧ in ⟦X⟧ by the function ⟦f⟧, one says that ⟦f⟧ maps ⟦x⟧ to ⟦y⟧, and this is commonly written ⟦y = f ( x ) .⟧ In this notation, ⟦x⟧ is the argument or variable of the function.

A specific element ⟦x⟧ of ⟦X⟧ is a value of the variable, and the corresponding element of ⟦Y⟧ is the value of the function at ⟦x⟧, or the image of ⟦x⟧ under the function. The image of a function, sometimes called its range, is the set of the images of all elements in the domain.

A function ⟦f⟧, its domain ⟦X⟧, and its codomain ⟦Y⟧ are often specified by the notation ⟦f : X → Y .⟧ One may write ⟦x ↦ y⟧ instead of ⟦y = f ( x )⟧, where the symbol ⟦↦⟧ (read 'maps to') is used to specify where a particular element ⟦x⟧ in the domain is mapped to by ⟦f⟧. This allows the definition of a function without naming. For example, the square function is the function ⟦x ↦ x^{2} .⟧

The domain and codomain are not always explicitly given when a function is defined. In particular, it is common that one might only know, without some (possibly difficult) computation, that the domain of a specific function is contained in a larger set. For example, if ⟦f : ℝ → ℝ⟧ is a real function, the determination of the domain of the function ⟦x ↦ 1 / f ( x )⟧ requires knowing the zeros of ⟦f.⟧ This is one of the reasons for which, in mathematical analysis, "a function from ⟦X⟧ to ⟦Y⟧ " may refer to a function having a proper subset of ⟦X⟧ as a domain. For example, a "function from the reals to the reals" may refer to a real-valued function of a real variable whose domain is a proper subset of the real numbers, typically a subset that contains a non-empty open interval. Such a function is then called a partial function.
A function ⟦f⟧ on a set ⟦S⟧ means a function from the domain ⟦S⟧, without specifying a codomain. However, some authors use it as shorthand for saying that the function is ⟦f: S → S⟧.
## Formal definition

The above definition of a function is essentially that of the founders of calculus, Leibniz, Newton and Euler. However, it cannot be formalized, since there is no mathematical definition of an "assignment". It is only at the end of the 19th century that the first formal definition of a function could be provided, in terms of set theory. This set-theoretic definition is based on the fact that a function establishes a relation between the elements of the domain and some (possibly all) elements of the codomain. Mathematically, a binary relation between two sets ⟦X⟧ and ⟦Y⟧ is a subset of the set of all ordered pairs ⟦( x , y )⟧ such that ⟦x ∈ X⟧ and ⟦y ∈ Y .⟧ The set of all these pairs is called the Cartesian product of ⟦X⟧ and ⟦Y⟧ and denoted ⟦X × Y .⟧ Thus, the above definition may be formalized as follows.

For every ⟦x⟧ in ⟦X⟧ there exists ⟦y⟧ in ⟦Y⟧ such that ⟦( x , y ) ∈ R .⟧

## Partial functions

Partial functions are defined similarly to ordinary functions, with the "total" condition removed. That is, a partial function from ⟦X⟧ to ⟦Y⟧ is a binary relation ⟦R⟧ between ⟦X⟧ and ⟦Y⟧ such that, for every ⟦x ∈ X ,⟧ there is at most one ⟦y⟧ in ⟦Y⟧ such that ⟦( x , y ) ∈ R .⟧
Using functional notation, this means that, given ⟦x ∈ X ,⟧ either ⟦f ( x )⟧ is in ⟦Y⟧, or it is undefined.

The set of the elements of ⟦X⟧ such that ⟦f ( x )⟧ is defined and belongs to ⟦Y⟧ is called the domain of definition of the function. A partial function from ⟦X⟧ to ⟦Y⟧ is thus an ordinary function that has as its domain a subset of ⟦X⟧ called the domain of definition of the function. If the domain of definition equals ⟦X⟧, one often says that the partial function is a total function.

In several areas of mathematics, the term "function" refers to partial functions rather than to ordinary (total) functions. This is typically the case when functions may be specified in a way that makes difficult or even impossible to determine their domain.

In calculus, a real-valued function of a real variable or real function is a partial function from the set ⟦ℝ⟧ of the real numbers to itself. Given a real function ⟦f : x ↦ f ( x )⟧ its multiplicative inverse ⟦x ↦ 1 / f ( x )⟧ is also a real function. The determination of the domain of definition of a multiplicative inverse of a (partial) function amounts to compute the zeros of the function, the values where the function is defined but not its multiplicative inverse.

Similarly, a function of a complex variable is generally a partial function whose domain of definition is a subset of the complex numbers ⟦ℂ⟧. The difficulty of determining the domain of definition of a complex function is illustrated by the multiplicative inverse of the Riemann zeta function: the determination of the domain of definition of the function ⟦z ↦ 1 / ζ ( z )⟧ is more or less equivalent to the proof or disproof of one of the major open problems in mathematics, the Riemann hypothesis.

In computability theory, a general recursive function is a partial function from the integers to the integers whose values can be computed by an algorithm (roughly speaking). The domain of definition of such a function is the set of inputs for which the algorithm does not run forever. A fundamental theorem of computability theory is that there cannot exist an algorithm that takes an arbitrary general recursive function as input and tests whether ⟦0⟧ belongs to its domain of definition (see Halting problem).

A multivariate function, multivariable function, or function of several variables is a function that depends on several arguments. Such functions are commonly encountered. For example, the position of a car on a road is a function of the time travelled and its average speed.

## Functions of more than one variable

In some cases the argument of a function may be an ordered pair of elements taken from some set or sets. For example, a function ⟦f⟧ can be defined as mapping any pair of real numbers ⟦( x , y )⟧ to the sum of their squares, ⟦x^{2} + y^{2}⟧. Such a function is commonly written as ⟦f ( x , y ) = x^{2} + y^{2}⟧ and referred to as "a function of two variables". Likewise one can have a function of three or more variables, with notations such as ⟦f ( w , x , y )⟧, ⟦f ( w , x , y , z )⟧.
## Other terms

A function may also be called a map or a mapping, but some authors make a distinction between the term "map" and "function". For example, the term "map" is often reserved for a "function" with some sort of special structure (for example maps of manifolds). In particular map may be used in place of homomorphism for the sake of succinctness (for example linear map or map from ⟦G⟧ to ⟦H⟧ instead of group homomorphism from ⟦G⟧ to ⟦H⟧). Some authors reserve the word mapping for the case where the structure of the codomain belongs explicitly to the definition of the function.
Some authors, such as Serge Lang, use "function" only to refer to maps for which the codomain is a subset of the real or complex numbers, and use the term mapping for more general functions.
In the theory of dynamical systems, a map denotes an evolution function used to create discrete dynamical systems. See also Poincaré map.
Whichever definition of map is used, related terms like domain, codomain, injective, continuous have the same meaning as for a function.
## Specifying a function

Given a function ⟦f⟧, by definition, to each element ⟦x⟧ of the domain of the function ⟦f⟧, there is a unique element associated to it, the value ⟦f ( x )⟧ of ⟦f⟧ at ⟦x⟧. There are several ways to specify or describe how ⟦x⟧ is related to ⟦f ( x )⟧, both explicitly and implicitly. Sometimes, a theorem or an axiom asserts the existence of a function having some properties, without describing it more precisely. Often, the specification or description is referred to as the definition of the function ⟦f⟧.
## By listing function values

On a finite set a function may be defined by listing the elements of the codomain that are associated to the elements of the domain. For example, if ⟦A = \{ 1 , 2 , 3 \}⟧, then one can define a function ⟦f : A → ℝ⟧ by ⟦f ( 1 ) = 2 , f ( 2 ) = 3 , f ( 3 ) = 4.⟧
## By a formula

Functions are often defined by an expression that describes a combination of arithmetic operations and previously defined functions; such a formula allows computing the value of the function from the value of any element of the domain.
For example, in the above example, ⟦f⟧ can be defined by the formula ⟦f ( n ) = n + 1⟧, for ⟦n ∈ \{ 1 , 2 , 3 \}⟧.

When a function is defined this way, the determination of its domain is sometimes difficult. If the formula that defines the function contains divisions, the values of the variable for which a denominator is zero must be excluded from the domain; thus, for a complicated function, the determination of the domain passes through the computation of the zeros of auxiliary functions. A quadratic function is a function that may be written ⟦f ( x ) = a x^{2} + b x + c ,⟧ where ⟦a, b, c⟧ are constants.

An elementary function is the same, with logarithms and exponential functions allowed.
## Inverse and implicit functions

A function ⟦f : X → Y ,⟧ with domain ⟦X⟧ and codomain ⟦Y⟧, is bijective, if for every ⟦y⟧ in ⟦Y⟧, there is one and only one element ⟦x⟧ in ⟦X⟧ such that ⟦y = f(x)⟧. In this case, the inverse function of ⟦f⟧ is the function ⟦f^{− 1} : Y → X⟧ that maps ⟦y ∈ Y⟧ to the element ⟦x ∈ X⟧ such that ⟦y = f(x)⟧. For example, the natural logarithm is a bijective function from the positive real numbers to the real numbers. It thus has an inverse, called the exponential function, that maps the real numbers onto the positive numbers.

If a function ⟦f : X → Y⟧ is not bijective, it may occur that one can select subsets ⟦E ⊆ X⟧ and ⟦F ⊆ Y⟧ such that the restriction of ⟦f⟧ to ⟦E⟧ is a bijection from ⟦E⟧ to ⟦F⟧, and has thus an inverse. The inverse trigonometric functions are defined this way. For example, the cosine function induces, by restriction, a bijection from the interval ⟦[0, π]⟧ onto the interval ⟦[-1, 1]⟧, and its inverse function, called arccosine, maps ⟦[-1, 1]⟧ onto ⟦[0, π]⟧. For example, the equation of the unit circle ⟦x^{2} + y^{2} = 1⟧ defines a relation on real numbers. If ⟦-1 < x < 1⟧ there are two possible values of ⟦y⟧, one positive and one negative. For ⟦x = ± 1⟧, these two values become both equal to 0. Otherwise, there is no possible value of ⟦y⟧. This means that the equation defines two implicit functions with domain ⟦[-1, 1]⟧ and respective codomains ⟦[0, +∞)⟧ and ⟦(-∞, 0]⟧.

## Using differential calculus

Many functions can be defined as the antiderivative of another function. This is the case of the natural logarithm, which is the antiderivative of ⟦1/x⟧ that is 0 for ⟦x = 1⟧. Another common example is the error function.

## Points from a rule

A function is a machine: put in a number, x, and out comes one number, f of x. For every input, take the pair made of the input and its output, and plot it as a point: x across, f of x up. The collection of all those points is the graph of the function. For f of x equals x squared, the points include nought, nought; one, one; two, four; and minus two, four. Together they make the U-shaped parabola.

## The vertical line test

A function gives exactly one output for each input. On a graph, that means that above any point on the horizontal axis there is at most one point of the graph. So if you imagine sweeping a vertical line across the picture, it must never cross the curve twice. A circle fails this test: a vertical line through the middle of the circle meets it at the top and at the bottom. A circle can still be described by an equation, but not as a single function of x.
## More than one input

Functions of two inputs, such as the height of a landscape at each point of a map, have graphs that are surfaces in three dimensions, rather like a range of hills. Those of more inputs cannot be drawn at all, but mathematicians still speak of their graphs, and reason about them by analogy.
## Graphs by ear

Graphs are usually seen, but they can be heard and described. Some modern programs sweep a tone from left to right, its pitch rising and falling with the curve, so that a listener can hear the shape. And a good description, such as the parabola falls from the upper left, touches its lowest point at the origin, and rises to the upper right, symmetrical about the vertical axis, conveys most of what the eye would see.
## Summary

The graph of a function is the set of points x, f of x. It passes the vertical line test: no vertical line crosses it twice. Functions of two inputs have surface graphs, and graphs can be heard as well as seen.

In geometry, a Cartesian coordinate system in a plane is a coordinate system that specifies each point uniquely by a pair of real numbers called coordinates, which are the signed distances to the point from two fixed perpendicular oriented lines, called coordinate lines, coordinate axes or just axes (plural of axis) of the system. The point where the axes meet is called the origin and has ⟦(0, 0)⟧ as coordinates. The axes directions represent an orthogonal basis. The combination of origin and basis forms a coordinate frame called the Cartesian frame.

Similarly, the position of any point in three-dimensional space can be specified by three Cartesian coordinates, which are the signed distances from the point to three mutually perpendicular planes. More generally, ⟦n⟧ Cartesian coordinates specify the point in an ⟦n⟧-dimensional Euclidean space for any dimension ⟦n⟧. These coordinates are the signed distances from the point to ⟦n⟧ mutually perpendicular fixed hyperplanes.

Cartesian coordinates are named for René Descartes, whose invention thereof in the 17th century revolutionized mathematics by allowing the expression of problems of geometry in terms of algebra and calculus. Using the Cartesian coordinate system, geometric shapes (such as curves) can be described by equations involving the coordinates of points of the shape. For example, a circle of radius 2, centered at the origin of the plane, may be described as the set of all points whose coordinates ⟦x⟧ and ⟦y⟧ satisfy the equation ⟦x^{2} + y^{2} = 4⟧; the area, the perimeter and the tangent line at any point can be computed from this equation by using integrals and derivatives, in a way that can be applied to any curve.

Cartesian coordinates are the foundation of analytic geometry, and provide enlightening geometric interpretations for many other branches of mathematics, such as linear algebra, complex analysis, differential geometry, multivariate calculus, group theory and more. A familiar example is the concept of the graph of a function. Cartesian coordinates are also essential tools for most applied disciplines that deal with geometry, including astronomy, physics, engineering and many more. They are the most common coordinate system used in computer graphics, computer-aided geometric design and other geometry-related data processing.
## History

The adjective Cartesian refers to the French mathematician and philosopher René Descartes, who published this idea in 1637 while he was resident in the Netherlands. It was independently discovered by Pierre de Fermat, who also worked in three dimensions, although Fermat did not publish the discovery. The French cleric Nicole Oresme used constructions similar to Cartesian coordinates well before the time of Descartes and Fermat.

Both Descartes and Fermat used a single axis in their treatments and have a variable length measured in reference to this axis. The concept of using a pair of axes was introduced later, after Descartes' La Géométrie was translated into Latin in 1649 by Frans van Schooten and his students. These commentators introduced several concepts while trying to clarify the ideas contained in Descartes's work.

The development of the Cartesian coordinate system played a fundamental role in the development of the calculus by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. The two-coordinate description of the plane was later generalized into the concept of vector spaces.
Many other coordinate systems have been developed since Descartes, such as the polar coordinates for the plane, and the spherical and cylindrical coordinates for three-dimensional space.
## One dimension
An affine line with a chosen Cartesian coordinate system is called a number line. Every point on the line has a real-number coordinate, and every real number represents some point on the line.

There are two degrees of freedom in the choice of Cartesian coordinate system for a line, which can be specified by choosing two distinct points along the line and assigning them to two distinct real numbers (most commonly zero and one). Other points can then be uniquely assigned to numbers by linear interpolation. Equivalently, one point can be assigned to a specific real number, for instance an origin point corresponding to zero, and an oriented length along the line can be chosen as a unit, with the orientation indicating the correspondence between directions along the line and positive or negative numbers. Each point corresponds to its signed distance from the origin (a number with an absolute value equal to the distance and a ⟦+⟧ or ⟦-⟧ sign chosen based on direction).

A geometric transformation of the line can be represented by a function of a real variable, for example translation of the line corresponds to addition, and scaling the line corresponds to multiplication. Any two Cartesian coordinate systems on the line can be related to each-other by a linear function (function of the form ⟦x ↦ a x + b⟧) taking a specific point's coordinate in one system to its coordinate in the other system. Choosing a coordinate system for each of two different lines establishes an affine map from one line to the other taking each point on one line to the point on the other line with the same coordinate.
## Two dimensions

A Cartesian coordinate system in two dimensions (also called a rectangular coordinate system or a Cartesian orthogonal coordinate system) is defined by an ordered pair of perpendicular lines (axes), a single unit of length for both axes, and an orientation for each axis. The point where the axes meet is taken as the origin for both, thus turning each axis into a number line. For any point P, a line is drawn through P perpendicular to each axis, and the position where it meets the axis is interpreted as a number. The two numbers, in that chosen order, are the Cartesian coordinates of P. The reverse construction allows one to determine the point P given its coordinates.

The first and second coordinates are called the abscissa and the ordinate of P, respectively; and the point where the axes meet is called the origin of the coordinate system. The coordinates are usually written as two numbers in parentheses, in that order, separated by a comma, as in (3, minus 10.5). Thus the origin has coordinates (0, 0), and the points on the positive half-axes, one unit away from the origin, have coordinates (1, 0) and (0, 1).

In mathematics, physics, and engineering, the first axis is usually defined or depicted as horizontal and oriented to the right, and the second axis is vertical and oriented upwards. (However, in some computer graphics contexts, the ordinate axis may be oriented downwards.) The axes may then be referred to as the X-axis and Y-axis. The choices of letters come from the original convention, which is to use the latter part of the alphabet to indicate unknown values. The first part of the alphabet was used to designate known values.

A Euclidean plane with a chosen Cartesian coordinate system is called a Cartesian plane. In a Cartesian plane, one can define canonical representatives of certain geometric figures, such as the unit circle (with radius equal to the length unit, and center at the origin), the unit square (whose diagonal has endpoints at (0, 0) and (1, 1)), the unit hyperbola, and so on.

The two axes divide the plane into four right angles, called quadrants. The quadrants may be named or numbered in various ways, but the quadrant where all coordinates are positive is usually called the first quadrant.

## Three dimensions

A Cartesian coordinate system for a three-dimensional space consists of an ordered triplet of lines (the axes) that go through a common point (the origin), and are pair-wise perpendicular; an orientation for each axis; and a single unit of length for all three axes. As in the two-dimensional case, each axis becomes a number line. For any point P of space, one considers a plane through P perpendicular to each coordinate axis, and interprets the point where that plane cuts the axis as a number. The Cartesian coordinates of P are those three numbers, in the chosen order. The reverse construction determines the point P given its three coordinates.
Alternatively, each coordinate of a point P can be taken as the distance from P to the plane defined by the other two axes, with the sign determined by the orientation of the corresponding axis.

Thus, the origin has coordinates ⟦(0, 0, 0)⟧, and the unit points on the three axes are ⟦(1, 0, 0)⟧, ⟦(0, 1, 0)⟧, and ⟦(0, 0, 1)⟧.

Standard names for the coordinates in the three axes are abscissa, ordinate and applicate. The axes may then be referred to as the x-axis, y-axis, and z-axis, respectively. Then the coordinate planes can be referred to as the xy-plane, yz-plane, and xz-plane.

In mathematics, physics, and engineering contexts, the first two axes are often defined or depicted as horizontal, with the third axis pointing up. In that case the third coordinate may be called height or altitude. The orientation is usually chosen so that the 90-degree angle from the first axis to the second axis looks counter-clockwise when seen from the point ⟦(0, 0, 1)⟧; a convention that is commonly called the right-hand rule.

## Higher dimensions

Since Cartesian coordinates are unique and non-ambiguous, the points of a Cartesian plane can be identified with pairs of real numbers; that is, with the Cartesian product ⟦ℝ^{2} = ℝ × ℝ⟧, where ⟦ℝ⟧ is the set of all real numbers. In the same way, the points in any Euclidean space of dimension n be identified with the tuples (lists) of n real numbers; that is, with the Cartesian product ⟦ℝ^{n}⟧.
## Generalizations

The concept of Cartesian coordinates generalizes to allow axes that are not perpendicular to each other, and/or different units along each axis. In that case, each coordinate is obtained by projecting the point onto one axis along a direction that is parallel to the other axis (or, in general, to the hyperplane defined by all the other axes). In such an oblique coordinate system the computations of distances and angles must be modified from that in standard Cartesian systems, and many standard formulas (such as the Pythagorean formula for the distance) do not hold (see affine plane).
## Notations and conventions

The Cartesian coordinates of a point are usually written in parentheses and separated by commas, as in (10, 5) or (3, 5, 7). The origin is often labelled with the capital letter O. This custom comes from a convention of algebra, which uses letters near the end of the alphabet for unknown values (such as the coordinates of points in many geometric problems), and letters near the beginning for given quantities.

These conventional names are often used in other domains, such as physics and engineering, although other letters may be used. For example, in a graph showing how a pressure varies with time, the graph coordinates may be denoted p and t. Each axis is usually named after the coordinate which is measured along it; so one says the x-axis, the y-axis, the t-axis, and so on

Another common convention for coordinate naming is to use subscripts, as (⟦x_{1}⟧, ⟦x_{2}⟧,..., ⟦x_{n}⟧) for the n coordinates in an n-dimensional space, especially when n is greater than 3 or unspecified. Some authors prefer the numbering (⟦x_{0}⟧, ⟦x_{1}⟧,..., ⟦x_{n−1}⟧). These notations are especially advantageous in computer programming: by storing the coordinates of a point as an array, instead of a record, the subscript can serve to index the coordinates.

In mathematical illustrations of two-dimensional Cartesian systems, the first coordinate (traditionally called the abscissa) is measured along a horizontal axis, oriented from left to right. The second coordinate (the ordinate) is then measured along a vertical axis, usually oriented from bottom to top. Young children learning the Cartesian system commonly learn the order to read the values before cementing the x-, y-, and z-axis concepts, by starting with 2D mnemonics (for example, 'Walk along the hall then up the stairs' akin to straight across the x-axis then up vertically along the y-axis).

Computer graphics and image processing, however, often use a coordinate system with the y-axis oriented downwards on the computer display. This convention developed in the 1960s (or earlier) from the way that images were originally stored in display buffers.

For three-dimensional systems, a convention is to portray the xy-plane horizontally, with the z-axis added to represent height (positive up). Furthermore, there is a convention to orient the x-axis toward the viewer, biased either to the right or left. If a diagram (3D projection or 2D perspective drawing) shows the x- and y-axis horizontally and vertically, respectively, then the z-axis should be shown pointing "out of the page" towards the viewer or camera. In such a 2D diagram of a 3D coordinate system, the z-axis would appear as a line or ray pointing down and to the left or down and to the right, depending on the presumed viewer or camera perspective. In any diagram or display, the orientation of the three axes, as a whole, is arbitrary. However, the orientation of the axes relative to each other should always comply with the right-hand rule, unless specifically stated otherwise. All laws of physics and math assume this right-handedness, which ensures consistency.

For 3D diagrams, the names "abscissa" and "ordinate" are rarely used for x and y, respectively. When they are, the z-coordinate is sometimes called the applicate. The words abscissa, ordinate and applicate are sometimes used to refer to coordinate axes rather than the coordinate values.
## Quadrants and octants

The axes of a two-dimensional Cartesian system divide the plane into four infinite regions, called quadrants, each bounded by two half-axes. These are often numbered from 1st to 4th and denoted by Roman numerals: I (where the coordinates both have positive signs), II (where the abscissa is negative − and the ordinate is positive +), III (where both the abscissa and the ordinate are −), and IV (abscissa +, ordinate −). When the axes are drawn according to the mathematical custom, the numbering goes counter-clockwise starting from the upper right ("north-east") quadrant.

Similarly, a three-dimensional Cartesian system defines a division of space into eight regions or octants, according to the signs of the coordinates of the points. The generalization of the quadrant and octant to an arbitrary number of dimensions is the orthant, and a similar naming system applies.

## In two dimensions

Fixing or choosing the x-axis determines the y-axis up to direction. Namely, the y-axis is necessarily the perpendicular to the x-axis through the point marked 0 on the x-axis. But there is a choice of which of the two half lines on the perpendicular to designate as positive and which as negative. Each of these two choices determines a different orientation (also called handedness) of the Cartesian plane.

The usual way of orienting the plane, with the positive x-axis pointing right and the positive y-axis pointing up (and the x-axis being the "first" and the y-axis the "second" axis), is considered the positive or standard orientation, also called the right-handed orientation.

A commonly used mnemonic for defining the positive orientation is the right-hand rule. Placing a somewhat closed right hand on the plane with the thumb pointing up, the fingers point from the x-axis to the y-axis, in a positively oriented coordinate system.
The other way of orienting the plane is following the left-hand rule, placing the left hand on the plane with the thumb pointing up.
When pointing the thumb away from the origin along an axis towards positive, the curvature of the fingers indicates a positive rotation along that axis.

Regardless of the rule used to orient the plane, rotating the coordinate system will preserve the orientation. Switching any one axis will reverse the orientation, but switching both will leave the orientation unchanged.
## In three dimensions

Once the x- and y-axes are specified, they determine the line along which the z-axis should lie, but there are two possible orientations for this line. The two possible coordinate systems which result are called 'right-handed' and 'left-handed'. The standard orientation, where the xy-plane is horizontal and the z-axis points up (and the x- and the y-axis form a positively oriented two-dimensional coordinate system in the xy-plane if observed from above the xy-plane) is called right-handed or positive.

The name derives from the right-hand rule. If the index finger of the right hand is pointed forward, the middle finger bent inward at a right angle to it, and the thumb placed at a right angle to both, the three fingers indicate the relative orientation of the x-, y-, and z-axes in a right-handed system. The thumb indicates the x-axis, the index finger the y-axis and the middle finger the z-axis. Conversely, if the same is done with the left hand, a left-handed system results.

In mathematics, the logarithm of a number is the exponent by which another fixed value, the base, must be raised to produce that number. For example, the logarithm of ⟦1000⟧ to base ⟦10⟧ is ⟦3⟧, because ⟦1000⟧ is ⟦10⟧ to the ⟦3⟧rd power: ⟦1000 = 10^{3} = 10 × 10 × 10⟧. More generally, if ⟦x = by⟧, then ⟦y⟧ is the logarithm of ⟦x⟧ to base ⟦b⟧, written ⟦logb x = y⟧, so ⟦log_{10} 1000 = 3⟧. As a single-variable function, the logarithm to base ⟦b⟧ is the inverse of exponentiation with base ⟦b⟧.

The logarithm base ⟦10⟧ is called the decimal or common logarithm and is commonly used in science and engineering. The natural logarithm has the number ⟦e ≈ 2.718⟧ as its base; its use is widespread in mathematics and physics because of its very simple derivative. The binary logarithm uses base ⟦2⟧ and is widely used in computer science, information theory, music theory, and photography. When the base is unambiguous from the context or irrelevant it is often omitted, and the logarithm is written ⟦log x⟧.

Logarithms were introduced by John Napier in 1614 as a means of simplifying calculations. They were rapidly adopted by navigators, scientists, engineers, surveyors, and others to perform high-accuracy computations more easily. Using logarithm tables, tedious multi-digit multiplication steps can be replaced by table look-ups and simpler addition. This is possible because the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms of the factors:
$$ \log_{b} ( x y ) = \log_{b} x + \log_{b} y
In plain words: it says that the two sides are equal. It uses a named function, such as sine, cosine or log, which turns one number into another.

The present-day notion of logarithms comes from Leonhard Euler, who connected them to the exponential function in the 18th century, and who also introduced the letter ⟦e⟧ as the base of natural logarithms.

Logarithmic scales reduce wide-ranging quantities to smaller scopes. For example, the decibel (dB) is a unit used to express ratio as logarithms, mostly for signal power and amplitude (of which sound pressure is a common example). In chemistry, pH is a logarithmic measure for the acidity of an aqueous solution. Logarithms are commonplace in scientific formulae, and in measurements of the complexity of algorithms and of geometric objects called fractals. They help to describe frequency ratios of musical intervals, appear in formulas counting prime numbers or approximating factorials, inform some models in psychophysics, and can aid in forensic accounting.

The concept of logarithm as the inverse of exponentiation extends to other mathematical structures as well. However, in general settings, the logarithm tends to be a multi-valued function. For example, the complex logarithm is the multi-valued inverse of the complex exponential function. Similarly, the discrete logarithm is the multi-valued inverse of the exponential function in finite groups; it has uses in public-key cryptography.

## History

The history of logarithms in seventeenth-century Europe saw the discovery of a new function that extended the realm of analysis beyond the scope of algebraic methods. The method of logarithms was publicly propounded by John Napier in 1614, in a book titled Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio (Description of the Wonderful Canon of Logarithms). Prior to Napier's invention, there had been other techniques of similar scopes, such as the prosthaphaeresis or the use of tables of progressions, extensively developed by Jost Bürgi around 1600. Napier coined the term for logarithm in Middle Latin, logarithmus, literally meaning 'ratio-number', derived from the Greek logos 'proportion, ratio, word' + arithmos 'number'.

The common logarithm of a number is the index of that power of ten which equals the number. Speaking of a number as requiring so many figures is a rough allusion to common logarithm, and was referred to by Archimedes as the "order of a number". The first real logarithms were heuristic methods to turn multiplication into addition, thus facilitating rapid computation. Some of these methods used tables derived from trigonometric identities. Such methods are called prosthaphaeresis.

Invention of the function now known as the natural logarithm began as an attempt to perform a quadrature of a rectangular hyperbola by Grégoire de Saint-Vincent, a Belgian Jesuit residing in Prague. Archimedes had written The Quadrature of the Parabola in the third century BC, but a quadrature for the hyperbola eluded all efforts until Saint-Vincent published his results in 1647. The relation that the logarithm provides between a geometric progression in its argument and an arithmetic progression of values, prompted A. A. de Sarasa to make the connection of Saint-Vincent's quadrature and the tradition of logarithms in prosthaphaeresis, leading to the term "hyperbolic logarithm", a synonym for natural logarithm. Soon the new function was appreciated by Christiaan Huygens, and James Gregory. The notation ⟦Log y⟧ was adopted by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in 1675, and the next year he connected it to the integral ⟦∫ \frac{d y}{y} .⟧
Before Euler developed his modern conception of complex natural logarithms, Roger Cotes had a nearly equivalent result when he showed in 1714 that

## Analytic properties

A deeper study of logarithms requires the concept of a function. A function is a rule that, given one number, produces another number. An example is the function producing the ⟦x⟧-th power of ⟦b⟧ from any real number ⟦x⟧, where the base ⟦b⟧ is a fixed number. This function is written as ⟦f ( x ) = b^{x}⟧. When ⟦b⟧ is positive and unequal to ⟦1⟧, we show below that ⟦f⟧ is invertible when considered as a function from the reals to the positive reals.
## Existence
Let ⟦b⟧ be a positive real number not equal to ⟦1⟧ and let ⟦f ( x ) = b^{x}⟧.

It is a standard result in real analysis that any continuous strictly monotonic function is bijective between its domain and range. This fact follows from the intermediate value theorem. Now, ⟦f⟧ is strictly increasing (for ⟦b > 1⟧), or strictly decreasing (for ⟦0 < b < 1⟧), is continuous, has domain ⟦ℝ⟧, and has range ⟦ℝ_{> 0}⟧. Therefore, ⟦f⟧ is a bijection from ⟦ℝ⟧ to ⟦ℝ_{> 0}⟧. In other words, for each positive real number ⟦y⟧, there is exactly one real number ⟦x⟧ such that ⟦b^{x} = y⟧.

We let ⟦\log_{b} : ℝ_{> 0} → ℝ⟧ denote the inverse of ⟦f⟧. That is, ⟦\log_{b} y⟧ is the unique real number ⟦x⟧ such that ⟦b^{x} = y⟧. This function is called the base-⟦b⟧ logarithm function or logarithmic function (or just logarithm).

Exponential growth occurs when a quantity grows as an exponential function of time. The quantity grows at a rate directly proportional to its present size. For example, when it is 3 times as big as it is now, it will be growing 3 times as fast as it is now.

In more technical language, its instantaneous rate of change (that is, the derivative) of a quantity with respect to an independent variable is proportional to the quantity itself. Often the independent variable is time. Described as a function, a quantity undergoing exponential growth is an exponential function of time, that is, the variable representing time is the exponent (in contrast to other types of growth, such as quadratic growth or cubic growth). Exponential growth is the inverse of logarithmic growth.

Terms like "exponential growth" are sometimes incorrectly interpreted as "rapid growth." Indeed, something that grows exponentially can in fact be growing slowly at first. Also, not all cases of growth at an always increasing rate are instances of exponential growth. For example the function ⟦f ( x ) = x^{3}⟧ grows at an ever increasing rate, but is much slower than growing exponentially. For example, when ⟦x = 1 ,⟧ it grows at 3 times its size, but when ⟦x = 10⟧ it grows at 30 percent of its size. If an exponentially growing function grows at a rate that is 3 times its present size, then it always grows at a rate that is 3 times its present size: when it is 10 times as big as it is now, it will grow 10 times as fast. On the other hand, functions may also grow faster than exponentially, for instance, the factorial or double exponential function.

If the constant of proportionality is negative, then the quantity decreases over time, and is said to be undergoing exponential decay instead. In the case of a discrete domain of definition with equal intervals, it is also called geometric growth or geometric decay since the function values form a geometric progression.
